newsitem.title: USA: Dlr slide continues to U.S. noon, Welteke stings.
newsitem.headline: Dlr slide continues to U.S. noon, Welteke stings.

text.p: The dollar stood mostly lower at U.S. midday after comments from Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke accelerated the greenback's overnight slippage, dealers and analysts said.

Welteke, on the fringes of a meeting of Germany's IG Metall trade union, said "...we cannot welcome a further rise in the dollar." News reports also quoted Welteke as saying he believed the dollar should trade near 1.70 marks and not exceed the 1.72 to 1.7350 range.
The greenback quickly fell more than a pfenning to a daily low of 1.7195 marks on news of Welteke's comments.

"The market was nervous this morning, initially because dollar/yen came off abruptly overnight. In the midst of that dollar vulnerability, the Welteke comments came in," said Audrey McNiff, vice president for foreign exchange sales at Goldman Sachs.
Bargain-hunters emerged to prop the dollar up, aided by an official clarification of Welteke's remarks, traders said.

A Bundesbank spokesman told Reuters Welteke "certainly did not give any levels at which the Bundesbank might no longer be happy with the dollar". He added that Welteke has repeatedly stated a dollar/mark rate "around 1.70" was not a problem.

"The Welteke comments, which apparently have been clarified, sent the dollar lower. But the attempt at damage control has people a little skeptical," said Mike Malpede, senior foreign exchange analyst at Refco Group, Ltd.
The dollar fell to 1.7219/24 marks at midday from 1.7300/05 at the open and 1.7325/35 at Monday's close. Dollar/yen edged lower to 125.40/50 from 125.62/72.

Dollar/yen slumped from 126.58/63 at Monday's close as the Nikkei-225 index exceeded 20,000 for the first time this year. Market players said a shift from Japanese government bonds to stocks and hints of Japanese recovery could cap dollar/yen.

"This may be a reflection that the (Japanese) economy is starting to bottom. The (Group of Seven) want the dollar to trade under a backdrop of fundamentals and we may be seeing them shift just a little," said Malpede.
Dealers said investors had bought the yen against a wide range of currencies overnight, notably the Australian dollar.

Overnight trading was dominated by a surge in the British pound, which hit a four-and-a-half-year high at 2.8330 marks. The Bank of England raised its official rate to 6.25 percent from 6.0 and was granted greater latitude to conduct monetary policy by new Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown.
The rate hike had been expected, but not until Wednesday, the original date for the BoE-Exchequer meeting, which was moved forward to Tuesday, dealers said.
"The speeded up meeting, the rate hike and the news of greater BoE independence, those are all certainly supportive of the (British) currency," said McNiff.
Sterling rose to $1.6375/85 from $1.6350/60 at the open after trading as high as $1.6404 in morning U.S. trade. The pound had rallied from $1.6225/35 at Monday's close.
Market players questioned whether sterling could continue to rise, despite talk of more rate hikes in the offing.
"Sterling is a little tricky. I don't think the new (Labor) government wants too strong a sterling," said Malpede.
In other trade, the dollar fell to 1.4610/20 Swiss francs from 1.4710/20 at the open. The greenback edged higher to Canadian $1.3775/80 from C$1.3770/75.
